author: Paul Stewart
introFa: کتاب «Brown Eyes» نوشته Paul Stewart یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح A2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Brown Eyes»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: 1899 STEWART ET AL. from the “jigsaw classroom” technique designed by Aronson and Bridgeman (1 979) to the stereotype negation training strategy recently introduced by Kawakami, Dovidio, Moll, Hermsen, and Russin (2000). One well-known, controversial strategy for reducing stereotyping, prejudice, and discrimination that has been conducted for over 30 years is Jane Elliott’s “blue-eyeshrown-eyes” prejudice simulation exercise (Peters, 1987). This exer- cise generally comprises blue-eyed individuals receiving discriminatory treat- ment, while brown-eyed individuals are treated preferentially, a procedure seemingly aimed at sensitizing participants to the emotional and behavioral con- sequences of being the object of discrimination. Elliott’s exercise was popular- ized through the documentary film “Eye of the Storm” (ABC News, 1970), segments of which are featured in the Discovering Psychology video series nar- rated by Philip Zimbardo (AnnenbergKPB, 1990). The exercise is also cited in social psychological texts such as Jones’ Prejudice and Racism (1997). In the 1990s, Elliott conducted an “Anatomy of Prejudice” tour, in which she intro- duced her exercise to international audiences. But is this renowned exercise effective in reducing prejudice? The present authors were surprised to discover no published empirical work assessing the effectiveness of Elliott’s exercise in reducing stereotyping, prejudice, and dis- crimination in adults. However, assessments have been conducted on variations of Elliott’s activity. One empirical study assessed the effects of the blue-eyes/ brown-eyes exercise on third-grade children, but contained methodological weak- nesses prohibiting a clear interpretation of the results (Weiner & Wright, 1973; see Byrnes & Kiger, 1990, for a summary of the study’s methodological short- comings). Byrnes and Kiger assessed the effectiveness of participating in a 3-hr abridged version of Elliott’s normally 8-hr activity on reducing stereotyping and prejudice in their college student participants. The authors reported mixed results for their assessment. No significant differences between the exercise and control groups were found for two prejudice measures: the Social Distance Scale (SDS; Bogardus, 1959) and requests to donate money to the “Martin Luther King, Jr., Fund” 1 year later. In fact, the only significant difference obtained in comparisons of the groups was that control group participants were more likely than were exercise group participants to condone discrimination to some degree, according to Byrnes and Kiger’s (1988) own Social Scenario scale. This weak evidence of the simulation’s effectiveness might suggest that the few benefits received by participating in the exercise are not worth the potential physical and emotional distress for both participants and facilitators of an exer- cise characterized by ridicule and unfair treatment of selected participants (Byrnes & Kiger, 1990). However, perhaps Byrnes and Kiger failed to find stronger support for the exercise’s efficacy because the exercise was not adminis- tered in such a way as to achieve full effectiveness. As previously noted, Byrnes and Kiger’s simulation lasted only 3 hr, whereas Elliott’s simulation generally

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1900 spans 8 hr and sometimes includes a follow-up session 1 month later. In addition, Byrnes and Kiger noted that their participants were a specialized sample: college students specializing in elementary education, 90% of whom were members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints, and 92% of whom were female. It is unclear whether religious background or gender composition would have had any substantial effects on the exercise’s effectiveness. However, Byrnes and Kiger suggested that these factors should be taken into account in interpreting their findings. And, finally, it is possible that more recently developed prejudice assessment measures (e.g., Dunton & Fazio’s, 1997, Motivation to Control Preju- diced Reactions scale [MCPR]) might be more sensitive in assessing effects of participating in the exercise. The present program evaluation assessed Elliott’s activity under conditions aimed at optimizing the possibility that effects of participating in Elliott’s activity on the reduction of stereotyping and prejudice could be detected. First, the full 8- hr activity was conducted by Jane Elliott herself, thereby ensuring that the activ- ity was conducted as intended by Elliott. Second, the participants were college students of diverse study areas randomly assigned to either the exercise group or a comparison group. Third, the effectiveness of the exercise was assessed using a variety of prejudice measures. Dunton and Fazio’s (1997) MCPR allowed a mea- sure of participants’ internal and external motivations to act in a prejudiced man- ner. The inclusion of the SDS (Bogardus, 1959) allowed comparison with Byrnes and Kiger’s (1990) findings. The widely used Modern Racism Scale (MRS; McConahay et al., 1981) was also included, as were questions concerning partic- ipants’ reactions to the exercise. In addition, attitudes toward Asian Americans and LatinoJLatina Americans, as well as toward African Americans, were assessed. Would these conditions produce findings suggesting that Elliott’s activ- ity is indeed effective in reducing stereotyping and prejudice, or would our find- ings replicate those of Byrnes and Kiger in suggesting that the activity’s fame is more pronounced than its effectiveness? In the next section, we summarize the details of the exercise before proceeding to elaborate on the materials and proce- dure utilized in our assessment. The Blue-EyedBrown-Eyes Exercise On February 26, 2000, Jane Elliott conducted her diversity training exercise with a group of college students. Prior to the exercise, the present authors obtained a randomly generated list of college students for possible participation in the exercise. These students were prescreened to have no prior knowledge of Elliott’s exercise. Potential participants were told that they would be assigned randomly either to a group in which they would participate in an exercise con- cerning intergroup relations or to a comparison group that would attend a presen- tation on intergroup relations.

1901 STEWART ET AL. Both groups were informed that they also would attend questionnaire sessions and would receive one course credit as compensation for their participation. Par- ticipants had to agree to be assigned to either the exercise or the comparison group in order to participate in the project. They indicated their agreement to par- ticipate in either group by signing a thorough informed consent form that cau- tioned about potential stress and physical discomfort associated with participation in the exercise group. From the pool of students who agreed to par- ticipate in either group, White students were randomly assigned to either the exercise or comparison group. Because of the small number of Students of Color at this college and the need for several students to represent the Students of Color group in the exercise, all African American, Asian American, Latinokatina, and Native American students were assigned to the exercise group. The actual exercise and related activities spanned an approximately 8-hr period, beginning at 7:30 a.m. on a Saturday. Upon arrival, Elliott sorted exercise participants into “Brown” and “Non-browdBlue” eye color groups. Students in the blue-eyed group were harassed by Elliott, made to wear neck collars, and sent to a room with an insufficient number of chairs where they waited for 1 hr and 23 min. During this time period, students in the brown-eyed group were shown to the activity room, given breakfast, and instructed by Elliott on how to act in a dis- criminatory manner toward the blue-eyed students. Elliott attempted to persuade brown-eyed students to discriminate against blue-eyed students for just one day, even if it was against their principles. Brown-eyed participants were also given half of the answers to a mock intelligence test that later would be administered to the entire group. Blue-eyed participants were then escorted to the room where the brown-eyed participants were already seated and were instructed to take seats in the middle of the room, with the brown-eyed participants facing them from either side. They were not given breakfast. For the next 4 hr and 25 min, the blue-eyed students were subjected to various discriminatory actions by Elliott and, occasionally, by the brown-eyed students. For example, blue-eyed students were made to stand one at a time and read aloud messages on posters placed around the room that displayed text and artwork derogating blue-eyed people. Any mistakes were crit- icized harshly by Elliott, with scolding of individual students in front of their peers sometimes lasting as long as 7 min. Blue-eyed students were also ridiculed for not performing as well as brown-eyed students on the mock intelligence test for which Elliott had given brown-eyed students half the answers. Other derisive actions directed by Elliott toward the blue-eyed students include the following: yelled at student about bad posture; commented on student’s “bedroom voice” and “cute butt”; criticized female participant for dying her hair blonde; mocked student for being unable to memorize a list of items orally relayed to her; told a student her behaviors were “evil”; and questioned blue-eyed students’ honesty. On numerous occasions, Elliott focused her attention on and ridiculed students

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1902 who made mistakes on a writing activity. At least two students cried in response to being the target of Elliott’s criticism, one of whom eventually left the room and ceased participation in the exercise. Frequently, Elliott prompted the brown-eyed students to assist in characteriz- ing the blue-eyed students as being less intelligent and other traits commonly used in stereotyping members of minority groups. A number of the students in the brown-eyed group complied. At the close of this period, Elliott announced that the exercise component of the day was concluded. All of the participants were then sent to lunch. Following lunch, the participants returned to the activity room where they discussed the activity for 1 hr and 28 min. Elliott handed out various materials, including recommended follow-up activities and readings concerning discrimina- tion and other issues related to intergroup relations. They then watched Elliott’s “Eye of the Storm” video for approximately 35 min. Following the video screen- ing, Elliott spent 7 min discussing the video with the participants and answering a few of the participants’ questions. Hors d’oeuvres were then served to all partici- pants. Follow-Up Sessions During the 3 weeks following the exercise, the college where the exercise was conducted held three optional follow-up sessions, which were attended by approximately half of the exercise participants. Counselors at the college where the exercise was conducted organized these sessions. The principal counselor reported that the overall purpose of the sessions was to provide student partici- pants with “a safe opportunity to express their thoughts, feelings, and reflections upon the exercise, orally and in writing.” The first session focused on having attendees write and discuss their emotional responses to the exercise. The key components of the second session were having participants practice listening skills, and write and discuss what they wished they had done differently on the day of the exercise. The final session focused on student participants’ feelings about Elliott’s upcoming follow-up session with the participants to be held 4 days later. Elliott returned on March 25, 2000, for her own follow-up discussion ses- sion with the participants. Assessment Within the 2-week period following Elliott’s March 25, 2000, follow-up session, participants in the exercise and comparison groups participated in questionnaire sessions during which they completed various measures of preju- dice and stereotyping. Because Elliott agreed to the assessment of her exercise only under the condition that no pretest or posttest measures be implemented

1903 STEWART ET AL. prior to her March 25 session, immediate assessment following the February 26 exercise was not possible. The Present Program Evaluation Program evaluations may be characterized by various goals (Isaac & Michael, 1997; Judd & Kenny, 1981; Rossi, Freeman, & Lipsey, 1999; Weiss, 1998). The goal of the present program evaluation is to assess and report the effectiveness of Elliott’s “blue-eyeshrown-eyes” diversity training exercise and, therefore, to provide information usehl to others considering implementing the exercise in their school or organization. It is important to note the precise nature of the present authors’ involvement with Elliott’s exercise and corporation in order to speak to the authors’ objectivity in this assessment, The present authors recruited and randomly assigned participants in the present assessment to the exercise and comparison groups and reminded participants of their scheduled exercise and assessment appointments through phone calls and notes sent via campus mail. The authors also conducted the assessments, but played no role in developing or implementing the activity. None of the authors were present when the exercise was conducted (the details of the exercise reported in this article were obtained from videotapes of the exercise). Four of the authors received aca- demic credit from the college in which they were enrolled for their role in facili- tating the activity. None of the authors received financial compensation from Elliott’s corporation for their work. Method Participants Recruitment. A randomly generated list of first-year, sophomore, and junior undergraduate students enrolled at a private liberal arts college in the north- eastern United States was obtained from the college’s registrar. These students were contacted about possibly participating in an intergroup relations project (described in general terms) for course credit. During recruitment, the project coordinators asked questions to ascertain whether potential participants were familiar with the exercise and to disqualify students with knowledge of the activity from participating in the project. A total of 47 students (34 White, 6 Afri- can American, 4 Latino/Latina, 2 Asian American, and 1 Native American) unfa- miliar with the exercise agreed to participate in the intergroup relations project and to be assigned randomly to either the exercise group or the comparison group. Potential participants were instructed that, if assigned to the exercise group, they would take part in an intergroup relations activity, complete various

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1904 questionnaires in a 1-hr session, and write a one-page reaction paper about their experiences with the project. They were further instructed that, if assigned to the comparison group, they would participate in a l-hr questionnaire session, after which they would attend and write a one-page reaction paper on a lecture/ discussion session on intergroup relations. The consent form signed by all partic- ipants included the following cautionary statement: You should be aware that the learning exercise may be a dificult experi- ence for some. Participants will take part in group discussions during which they may be exposed to harsh comments and uncomfortable condi- tions. . . . If you have a medical condition that might be aggravated by stressful situations or feel that you should avoid stressful situations at the present time, do not sign up for this project. The consent form also stated that participants in both groups would receive one academic credit for their participation and that they could discontinue participa- tion at any time without penalty. Group composition. Of the 34 White students who agreed to participate, 22 were randomly assigned to the exercise group and 12 to the comparison group. Of the 22 White students assigned to the exercise group, 16 participated in the exercise. Of these 16 participants, 13 later completed the prejudice measures. Of the 12 White students randomly assigned to the comparison group, 1 1 completed the prejudice measures. Because of the small number of Students of Color enrolled at the college and the importance of a number of Students of Color par- ticipating in the exercise, all of the recruited Students of Color were assigned to the exercise group. With the exception of 1 of the 4 Latino/Latina students, all 13 of the Students of Color assigned to the exercise group participated in the exer- cise. With the exception of 2 African American students and 1 Latino student, all of the Students of Color who participated in the exercise also attended the ques- tionnaire sessions. On the day of the exercise, Jane Elliott further subdivided exercise partici- pants into two groups based on eye color. Students with brown eyes would receive preferential treatment, whereas students whose eyes were classified by Elliott as blue would be the recipients of discriminatory treatment. Although the project coordinators intended all Students of Color to be assigned to the brown- eye color group, regardless of eye color, one Student of Color with green eyes was inadvertently assigned to the blue-eye color group. Reasons for attrition. For reporting purposes, we later contacted the 6 White students who had been assigned to the exercise group but who did not participate in the exercise to determine the reasons for their nonparticipation. One of these students had contacted the project coordinators the day before the exercise to report that she would not be able to attend for health reasons. Another of these

1905 STEWART ET AL. students contacted the project coordinators the day after the exercise to apologize for not attending and to explain that she had been unsure where to meet for the exercise. The remaining 4 students reported scheduling conflicts as the reason for their nonparticipation (e.g., a play rehearsal scheduled for the day of the exer- cise). To further assess these students’ present attitudes toward participating in the activity, we asked the students if they would be willing to participate in the exercise the following semester if it were conducted again at that time (although there were actually no plans to conduct the exercise again). Three of the 6 stu- dents stated that they would be interested in participating. Two students expressed concern about the time commitment during a particularly busy semes- ter, with one of these students reporting that he might still be interested in partic- ipating and the other stating that she would not be interested in participating. The sixth student had heard about the exercise from friends and therefore was no longer eligible to participate in the exercise. Because the exercise was conducted on one day only, it was not possible for students who missed the exercise to make up the exercise at another time. In contrast, we were able to reschedule questionnaire sessions for participants from both the exercise and comparison group who failed to show up for their originally scheduled sessions. Of the 3 White students who participated in the exercise but who did not complete the assessment, 1 failed to show up for two scheduled questionnaire sessions and could not be reached to schedule another makeup session. The 2 other White students who participated in the exercise but not the questionnaire session stated that they did not want to continue participat- ing in the project because they had found the exercise itself to be so distressing that they wanted no further involvement in the project. All 3 of these students had been assigned to the blue-eye color group that was the object of discrimination during the exercise. The 1 student from the comparison group who did not com- plete the prejudice measures could not be reached to schedule the questionnaire session. Materials and Procedure From 4 to 6 weeks following the day of the exercise, participants in both the exercise and comparison groups completed various prejudice assessment mea- sures in a l-hr questionnaire session. The assessment measures were completed on separate computer stations by 2 participants at a time. All participants com- pleted informed consent forms at the start of the questionnaire session and were debriefed at the close of the session. The assessment sessions originally were scheduled to be conducted during the 2 weeks immediately following the exercise, a plan that had been approved by Elliott several months prior to the exercise. However, on the evening prior to the exercise, Elliott previewed some of the assessment measures and expressed second thoughts about allowing her

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1906 activity to be assessed empirically. She stated that she was particularly concerned that participating in the assessment might influence participants’ behavior during the follow-up discussion session scheduled to be held 4 weeks after the activity. It was agreed, therefore, to delay the assessment until after the follow-up discus- sion session. Measures. Degree of prejudice was assessed using three separate measures, each of which proved to have adequate reliability for the present population: an updated version of the SDS (Bogardus, 1925; a = .94), the MRS (McConahay et al., 1981; a = .74), and the MCPR (Dunton & Fazio, 1997; a = .78). The SDS required participants to indicate on 9-point Likert-type scales their will- ingness to have various types of relationships (e.g., friend, neighbor, teacher, romantic date) with members of the following groups: Asian Americans, White Americans, Latino/Latina Americans, and African Americans. We treated rat- ings of each group as a separate subscale (e.g., the SDS-Asian American sub- scale). The MRS was designed to assess participants’ degree of modem racism through assessment items cast as political opinion queries (e.g., “Over the past few years, African Americans have gotten more than they deserve economi- cally’’) rated on 9-point Likert-type scales. The MCPR also comprised items rated on 9-point scales and measured individuals’ motivation to control their expression of prejudice as a result of concern with appearing prejudiced to themselves or to others or because of a desire to avoid dispute. Note that whereas higher scores on the SDS indicate more positive attitudes toward the groups rated and higher scores on the MCPR indicate greater motivation to avoid acting in a prejudiced manner, higher numbers on the MRS indicate greater modern racism. Participants completed the prejudice assessment measures on computers. Par- ticipants in the exercise condition also completed a brief pen-and-paper question- naire surveying their positive and negative reactions to the activity. Students of Color were not asked to complete either the MRS or the MCPR, given that these measures were normed to assess prejudice for White individuals. However, Stu- dents of Color did complete the SDS (Bogardus, 1959) and the pen-and-paper measure of their reactions to the activity. Correlations among prejudice assessment measures. The SDS-African American, SDS-Latino/Latina, and SDS-Asian American subscales were all highly intercorrelated (all rs > 3 5 , allps < .0001). However, the SDS-White subscale was not significantly correlated with any of the other SDS subscales, nor with the MRS or the MCPR. Participants who showed higher degrees of prejudice on the MRS also showed more prejudice (less positive attitudes) on the SDS-African American subscale (r = -.46, p < .Ol), the SDS-Latino/Latina subscale (r = -.57, p < .002), and the SDS-Asian American subscale (r = -.52, p < ,005). The MCPR was correlated with the MRS ( r = -.47,p < .Ol), but not with any of the SDS subscales.

Results Social Distance Did Whites who had participated in the exercise report significantly greater comfort with the possibility of various social relationships with African Ameri- cans, Latinos/Latinas, and Asian Americans than Whites who had not partici- pated in the exercise? We examined the relationship between condition and SDS (Bogardus, 1959) scores using a MANOVA. Scores on the SDS-African Ameri- can, SDS-Latino/Latina, and SDS-Asian American subscales were entered into the MANOVA, with condition entered as a between-subjects factor and score on the SDS-White subscale entered as a covariate. The MANOVA yielded a signifi- cant main effect for condition, F(3, 19) = 3 . 7 4 , ~ < .03, q2 = .37, with White par- ticipants in the exercise group reporting greater comfort with relationships with members of other groups than Whites in the comparison group. In addition, the corresponding univariate tests were significant for the SDS-Asian American sub- scale, F(1, 21) = 9 . 0 3 , ~ < .007, q2 = .30; and the SDS-LatinoILatina subscale, F(1,21) = 4 . 6 6 , ~ < .05, q2 = .18; and marginally significant for the SDS-African American subscale, F(1, 21) = 3 . 2 9 , ~ = .08, q2 = .14. No other effects were sig- nificant. Social distance ratings for Whites in the exercise and comparison groups and for African Americans in the exercise group are provided in Table 1.

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1908 As previously stated, there were not enough Students of Color in the pop- ulation of the college where the exercise was conducted to include student participants from this group in both the exercise and comparison groups. There- fore, we could not analyze the SDS scores of Students of Color by condition. Because of identifiability concerns, SDS scores for the small number of Latino/ Latina and Asian American participants in the exercise group are not included in Table 1. Modern Racism Was participation in the exercise related to White participants’ degree of modern racism? The pattern of MRS (McConahay et al., 1981) scores for Whites in the exercise and comparison groups was in the predicted direction, with Whites in the comparison group displaying greater modern racism ( M = 1.96) than Whites in the exercise group (M= 1 S4). However, a multivariate anal- ysis of target items on the MRS, with condition entered as a between-subjects factor, failed to demonstrate a significant main effect of condition, F(7, 15) = 1.09, p = .42. Motivation to Control Prejudiced Reactions A MANOVA incorporating all 17 MCPR (Dunton & Fazio, 1997) items, with condition and participant gender entered as between-subjects factors, reveals marginally greater reported motivation to control prejudiced reactions by Whites in the exercise group ( M = 5.28) than by Whites in the comparison group ( M = 4.59), F( 17, 3) = 5.85, p = .085, q2 = .97. Forward stepwise logistic regression was then conducted to identify the MCPR items that best predicted condition membership (exercise or comparison group). Regression results indicate that the overall model of two predictors (“I get angry with myself when I have a thought or feeling that might be considered prejudiced”; and “Going through life wony- ing about whether you might offend someone is just more trouble than it’s worth,” reverse scored) was statistically reliable in distinguishing condition membership (-2 log likelihood = 20.34), x2(2, N = 23) = 11.16, p < .004. The model correctly classified 78% of the cases. Wald statistics indicate that the item “I get angry with myself when I have a thought or feeling that might be consid- ered prejudiced” significantly predicted condition (M agreement with this item was 8.00 for the exercise group and 5.70 for the comparison group; p < .04, Wald significance value = 4.32, df = 1). The Cox and Snell R2 reveals that this item accounted for 26% of the variance. The reverse-scored item “Going through life worrying about whether you might offend someone is just more trouble than it’s worth” proved to be a marginally significant predictor (M disagreement with this item was 5.23 for the exercise group and 3.00 for the comparison group; p = .07,

1909 STEWART ET AL. Wald significance value = 3.30, df = 1). Full-model logistic regression similarly reveals significant effects only for the items “I get angry . . .” (p < .02, Wald sig- nificance value = 6.14, df = 1) and “Going through life worrying . . .” (p < .03, Wald significance value = 4.74, df = 1). Exploratory mediation analyses exam- ined whether exercise participants’ lower prejudice scores on the SDS-Asian American and SDS-Latino/Latina subscales might be mediated by their greater anger toward themselves when acting in a prejudiced manner, but yielded no sup- port for this mediation path. Additional Analyses of the Prejudice Measures Effects associated with attending follow-up sessions. As previously stated, the questionnaire sessions were conducted several weeks after the exercise, during which time some participants attended one or more of three optional follow-up sessions. Consequently, the results reported in the previous sections could be a result of participation in either the exercise group, the follow-up sessions, or both. We conducted additional analyses on the exercise group data to examine the relationship between attending follow-up sessions and prejudice level. How- ever, it is important to keep in mind possible selection factors associated with participants choosing or not choosing to attend the optional follow-up sessions. A chi-square analysis including the variables eye-color group and “Attended at least one session (Yes or No)” indicates no difference in the percentage of partic- ipants from the two eye-color groups who attended at least one of the follow-up sessions. However, a separate chi-square analysis indicates that Students of Color were significantly more likely than were White students to have attended at least one of the follow-up sessions, x2( 1, N = 22) = 5.7 1, p < .02, q2 = .5 1. We next analyzed whether there was a correlation between number of follow- up sessions attended (range = 0 to 3) and responses on the prejudice measures. These analyses produced no significant differences on the overall MRS and MCPR scales or the SDS subscales as a function of number of follow-up sessions attended. Because we were not allowed to conduct assessments prior to the fol- low-up sessions, a causal relationship between attending follow-up sessions and level of prejudice could not be determined. Therefore, we conducted additional analyses partialing out the effects of follow-up session attendance on prejudice measure scores. All of the effects that reached significance in the primary anal- yses were also significant in analyses adjusting for the effects of the number of follow-up sessions attended variable. Estimating effects of attrition. Shadish, Hu, Glaser, Kownacki, and Wong (1 998) introduced procedures to assess the possible effects of attrition in random- ized experiments. We adapted one of these procedures to estimate the effects of attrition in the present assessment. Prejudice measure scores were analyzed once again using data sets that included experimenter-generated data for the 6 White

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1910 students assigned to the exercise group who, for various reasons reported previ- ously in this paper, did not attend the exercise. In three separate data sets, preju- dice measure data for the 6 missing exercise group participants were replaced with (a) the comparison group’s mean scores on each of the prejudice measures, (b) the most prejudiced scores given by participants in the exercise group on each of the prejudice measures, and (c) the most prejudiced scores given by partici- pants in either the exercise or the comparison group on each of the prejudice measures. The generated data for each data set were designed to work against our hypothesis of lower prejudice for the activity group. Significant results obtained despite these added data would provide some assurance that our findings were not a result of the attrition of particularly prejudiced individuals from the exercise group. The first data set was constructed under the assumption that the 6 missing exercise group participants would not have performed differently on the preju- dice measures than the average comparison group participant. The second data set was built on the assumption that the 6 missing exercise participants would have exhibited as much prejudice as the most prejudiced individual who attended the exercise. The third data set assumed that all 6 of the missing exercise partici- pants would have shown as much prejudice as any individual in either the exer- cise or comparison groups. The third data set offered the biggest challenge to our hypotheses and, in fact, none of the significant effects reported were able to withstand the addition of experimenter-generated data for 6 members of the exercise group with prejudice scores equal to the most prejudiced responses given by any participant in the assessment. However, the key significant effects reported in this manuscript con- tinued to be significant in analyses of both the first and second experimenter- generated data sets. Reactions to Participating in the Exercise At the close of the questionnaire session, participants in the exercise group completed a questionnaire about their experiences in the exercise. In addition to two open-ended questions concerning their positive and negative reactions to the exercise, exercise participants also responded to two Yes/No questions: “Are you glad that you participated in the activity?’ and “Would you recommend partici- pating in the activity to others?’ Of the 9 Students of Color who completed this form, all 9 indicated that they were glad that they themselves had participated in the activity, and 8 of them reported that they would recommend participating in the activity to others. Of the 10 White students who completed this form, 9 reported that they were glad that they themselves had participated in the activity. However, only 5 out of 10 reported that they would definitely recommend the activity to others. Out of 10 White participants, 4 reported that they were unsure

191 1 STEWART ET AL. about recommending the activity to others, and I did not answer this question (although the participant answered the question concerning his or her own feel- ings about participating in the activity). A MANOVA comparing the responses of Students of Color and White students on these two items indicated a weak trend for Students of Color to report feeling more positive about the exercise than did White students, F(2, 15) = 2 . 2 4 , ~ = .14, q2 = .23. We next compared the responses to these two survey items of students in the exercise who were discriminated against (7 White students and 1 Student of Color in the blue eye-color group) and those who were not (3 White students and 8 Students of Color in the brown eye-color group). Of the 11 participants in the brown eye-color group, which was not discriminated against, 10 reported both that they were glad that they participated in the activity and that they would rec- ommend the activity to others. Of the 8 participants in the blue eye-color group, which was discriminated against, all 8 reported that they were glad that they themselves had participated in the activity, but only 3 reported that they would definitely recommend the activity to others. A MANOVA of the two items, with eye-color group included as a between-subjects factor, indicated that the pattern of responses to these two survey items differed marginally for students in the two eye-color groups, F(2, 15) = 3.02, p = .079, q 2 = .29. Participants in the two eye-color groups were equally likely to report being glad that they participated in the activity, F < 1. However, participants in the eye color group that was not discriminated against were significantly more likely than participants in the dis- criminated group to report that they would recommend the activity to others, F(I, 16) = 6 . 0 2 , ~ < .03, q2 = .27. It is important to note that the findings reported in this section do not include responses from the 2 White exercise group participants who stated that they chose to discontinue participation in the project because they found the exercise too distressing. One of these individuals was so negatively affected by participat- ing in the exercise that she broke off participation during the first 2 hr of the exer- cise, leaving the room in obvious distress. These participants would almost certainly have indicated that they would have preferred not to have participated in the activity and probably would not have recommended the activity to others. Discussion Is the Jane Elliott diversity training exercise-in which participants are sub- jected to sneering looks, scalding criticism, group humiliation, and food depri- vation for an extended period of time-effective in reducing prejudice in its participants? According to the present program evaluation, the answer is a qualified “Yes.” With the SDS (Bogardus, 1959) measure, White college students randomly assigned to participate in the diversity training exercise were found to hold significantly more positive attitudes toward Asian Americans, LatinoJLatina

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1912 Americans, and, to a marginal degree, African Americans after participating in the exercise than did their White peers randomly assigned to the comparison group. Furthermore, Whites in the exercise group were significantly more likely than Whites in the comparison group to report on the MCPR (Dunton & Fazio, 1997) that they felt angry toward themselves when experiencing a prejudiced thought or feeling. No overall differences were found with the MRS. The significant findings for the SDS in the present program evaluation stand in contrast to the findings with this scale reported by Byrnes and Kiger in their 1990 program evaluation of an abridged version of the prejudice simulation exer- cise. The difference in findings between the two assessments suggests that the full-length diversity training exercise was more effective than the shortened ver- sion of the exercise. However, it is also possible that the significant effects in the present experiment are a result of the time delay between the exercise and the assessment of the exercise’s effectiveness. At Elliott’s request, several weeks passed between the exercise and the assessment. Conversely, Byrnes and Kiger implemented all of their assessment measures soon after the completion of the exercise (with the only long-term measure having insufficient participants for analyses). Perhaps participating in the activity produces more positive results over time, after participants have returned to their daily routines and found them- selves sensitized to the issues addressed in the exercise. It is also possible that the optional follow-up sessions in which participants had the opportunity to further discuss discrimination issues could have buttressed the impact of Elliott’s exer- cise. However, the similarity in responses on the assessment measure of partici- pants who attended versus did not attend the follow-up sessions suggests that the effects reported in this evaluation are more a result of participation in Elliott’s activity than the follow-up discussion sessions. Using their Social Scenarios scale, Byrnes and Kiger did find some evidence that the abridged exercise was effective in increasing participants’ “professed willingness to act in antidiscrimi- natory ways” (p. 351). Perhaps the most compelling explanation of the different findings on the SDS for the present program evaluation and that of Byrnes and Kiger (1 990) is that the present assessment examined participants’ comfort with African Americans, LatinosILatinas, and Asian Americans as well as Whites, whereas Byrnes and Kiger assessed only participants’ comfort with African Americans. As previously reported, the present program evaluation found much stronger effects of the exer- cise on White participants’ comfort with Asian Americans and LatinodLatinas than with African Americans. In fact, the effect of the exercise in reducing preju- dice toward African Americans was only marginally significant, whereas the effects for Asian Americans and LatinodLatinas were consistently significant. Perhaps Byrnes and Kiger would have found significant effects on the SDS had they included Asian Americans and LatinodLatinas, in addition to African Americans, as target groups.

191 3 STEWART ET AL. In the present program evaluation, we did not predict the weaker effects of the exercise on prejudice toward African Americans. Therefore, we can only speculate about the causes of this finding. Perhaps participants felt stronger reac- tance against the exercise with regard to African Americans compared with other groups because the exercise seemed to be more related to the discriminatory experiences of African Americans. The water fountains and bathroom doors marked “Brown Eyes Only” were strongly reminiscent of the Jim Crow policies of which many students may be aware. We would have anticipated that this simi- larity would have resulted in stronger effects for the African American group. But perhaps the heavyhanded nature of the exercise induced reactance instead. Alternatively, perhaps both the exercise and comparison groups thought of African Americans more than other groups when signing up for a study on inter- group relations, and therefore both groups attempted to respond in socially desir- able ways to questions about this group. Therefore, differences between White exercise and comparison group participants on questions concerning African Americans would be minimized as a result of social desirability concerns. The particularly strong findings for Asian Americans might be related to this group continuing to be perceived as the model minority, and therefore attitudes toward them being more susceptible to positive change. Further research is needed to elucidate the reasons for the stronger effects of the exercise in reducing preju- dice toward Asian Americans and LatinodLatinas compared with African Amer- icans, as identified by the present program evaluation. For now, it is interesting to note the greater variability for White participants in both the exercise and com- parison groups in their SDS ratings for African Americans versus the other rated groups. Other factors that might have impacted our general findings include the par- ticipants’ status as college students and the particularly liberal student environ- ment of the college attended by the participants. Prior research at the liberal arts college attended by the present participants indicated that these students provided significantly more progressive responses on various intergroup attitude measures than did students at a large state university (Stewart, Vassar, Sanchez, & David, 2000). Consequently, we were at risk for finding ceiling effects on the measures of attitudes toward other groups employed in the present study, thus preventing identification of differences between the exercise and comparison groups. From this standpoint, the significant differences obtained on several of the key preju- dice measures in the present study are particularly notable. However, it could also be argued that students from this college might be particularly receptive to the messages of the exercise and might show especially strong effects. Sample characteristics such as the particularly liberal nature of the present participants and the identification of most of the predominantly female sample in Byrnes and Kriger’s (1990) study as members of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints should be considered when making comparisons across studies. Different

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 1914 findings might also be expected for participants undergoing a less thorough informed consent procedure and for younger participants, although ethical con- siderations would most likely preclude exploring these possibilities. The significant findings in the present program evaluation are all the more impressive given the 4- to 6-week delay between the exercise and the assessment and the lower than desired number of participants. A number of the participants commented positively on the activity on open-ended questions concerning partic- ipants’ views on the “positive and/or negative” aspects of the activity, although some qualified their positive reactions by noting the stress, discomfort, and other possible negative ramifications of participating in the activity. Selected positive and mixed comments on the exercise are: I realized how responsible I am for the problem of racism today. I wanted to try to forget some of the things that were said or done on the day of the experi- ment, but I guess that’s what made it so effective. I’m more aware of the White advantages and power that exist in our society. I didn’t realize the degree to which it is true before the project. (White male, brown eyed) It was in some ways an eye-opening experience, certainly an emotionally charged one. (Asian American male, brown eyed) Although I do not agree wholeheartedly with the activity, one of the posi- tive aspects for me was that someone, especially a White person, is taking initiative to address racism, not in the “political” sphere, as we are accus- tomed to seeing, but rather addressing racialized/racist thinking in the area of personal interaction, showing how individual attitudes become group attitudes responsible for oppression of those who do not belong to said group. . . . One thing I noticed is that some “blue eye people” who participated in the activity said “Hello” to me in passing when they saw me on campus when they never did. I wondered was it because the activity made a “dent,” or because we were together in that room for over

However, I can’t say it’s negative because I don’t know what was going on in those “blue minds” of theirs. A lot of repressed or forgotten memories creeped back up, racism I’ve experi- enced, did not hurt me. 1 feel I have matured in dealing with racism and not letting it affect me too emotionally. Otherwise, the experience was a positive one, involving a jarring realignment of a number of precepts on race and allowing an opportunity to re-evaluate a number of concepts involving self-identity, social dynamics, and power structures. Despite considerable emotional strain, I feel the experience was worthwhile. This is why I do not consider the difficulty of the project a negative aspect. (White male, blue eyed) The Role of Negative Emotion in Reducing Versus Enhancing Prejudice While the more positive attitudes toward members of minority groups dem- onstrated through scores on the SDS would seem to be an unequivocally positive finding, the findings on the MCPR are less clear. Is it really a step in the right direction to subject participants to an activity that will increase their feelings of anger toward themselves, even if that anger is caused by their desire to be non- prejudiced? Several of the present authors who helped to recruit participants in the project, as well as at least one counselor consulted about the project, expressed concerns about the negative emotions engendered in students who par- ticipated in the exercise. The original frustration-aggression hypothesis proposed by Dollard, Doob, Miller, Mowrer, and Sears (1939) posited that frustration in obtaining desired goals could lead to increased aggression. Berkowitz (1989, 1990) presented

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 191 6 evidence in support of his reformulation of the fiustration-aggression hypothesis in which he argued that thwartings, as aversive events, evoke negative affect (any feeling that people typically seek to lessen or eliminate), and it is this negative feeling that generates the aggressive inclinations. . . . It is not the exact nature of the aversive incident that is important but how intense the resulting nega- tive affect is. (Berkowitz, 1989, p. 68) Relatedly, physical discomfort (e.g., the food deprivation experienced by blue- eyed participants in the exercise) also has been found to lead to an increased likelihood of angry aggression toward available targets, even toward people who played no role in inducing the physical discomfort (Berkowitz & Thome, 1987). Even White participants who reported an overall positive evaluation of Elliott’s exercise often qualified their appraisal by noting that the exercise was an intensely aversive experience. And White participants’ MCPR responses suggest that negative affect associated with the activity is measurable even several weeks after the initial aversive experience. Therefore, it is possible that the aversive nature of the activity, particularly for blue-eyed Whites, might, in the long term, lead to Whites experiencing increased aggression. These aggressive inclinations might even be directed toward the very groups for whom reduction of prejudice and discriminatory treatment was the goal, if participants resort to blaming the victims to justify the unfair treatment these individuals receive in order to reduce their own negative emotions associated with awareness of this injustice (Festinger, 1957). Conversely, social psychologists such as Dovidio and Gaertner (I 999) have argued that the increased negative affect associated with prompting individuals to examine inconsistencies between their nonprejudiced values and their often sub- tle, and perhaps even unconscious, prejudiced thoughts and actions can play a key role in motivating these individuals to develop more positive intergroup atti- tudes. However, much of this work focuses on nonprejudiced motivations stem- ming from feelings of personal guilt, rather than anger. It is possible that anger might foster less self-analysis than guilt, thereby rendering anger less effective than guilt in prompting awareness of dissonant values that might lead to reduced prejudice. Tatum (1 997) concurs with Dovidio and Gaertner (1 999) that negative emo- tions experienced by White individuals as a result of confronting racism within themselves and in their society can motivate these individuals to work toward a less prejudiced self and society. In fact, she argued that anger toward racism within oneself and society is a key stage along White individuals’ journey toward a positive White identity in which they perceive Whiteness in a positive light,

1917 STEWART ET AL. while nonetheless acknowledging and opposing the realities of racism. However, Tatum points to the dangers of this stage as well: Sometimes poorly organized antiracism workshops or other educational experiences can create a scenario that places participants at risk for get- ting stuck in their anger. Effective consciousness-raising about racism must also point the way toward constructive action. When people don’t have the tools for moving forward, they tend to return to what is familiar, often becoming more vigorous in their defense of the racial status quo than they were initially. (p. 105) Several exercise participants, including some who felt positive about the activity overall, expressed related concerns about the activity in response to the open- ended question inquiring about their “positive and/or negative” responses to the exercise. Selected excerpted comments include the following: makes people upset; doesn’t change much; too negative for me. (White male, brown eyed) As a Blue Eye, I was uncomfortable and on edge. I found myself easily angered by anything Jane Elliott said. I felt frustrated and helpless to stop her charade (she was good at her job). In some small way, I see everyone differently. I recognize better now where minorities are coming from socially and therefore psychologically. More than anything else, I am bet- ter conditioned to recognize racism when I cross it. (White male, blue- eyed) I respond negatively to aspects of Jane’s methodologies. I also feel that we should have been debriefed by Jane even more after the Saturday (end of day). Most of my negativity is regarding specifics. I feel some of it was unethical, however, there were so many positive responses I can only believe that the positive outweighs the negatives. . . . I’ve had a few night- mares, but this is typical. . . . I’m really curious to know what the psychol- ogy teachers think-especially regarding the ethics. Do the means justify the ends? I think so for me, but I still can’t accept this program . . . there has got to be a better way to learn. I feel the races were further separated by this exercise. This is my biggest problem. This is the big negative ram- ification. I feel less connected to the Blacks on campus now (instead of feeling as though we are all so similar on the inside). (White female, blue eyed) Although the tension in the room was strong and uncomfortable at times, I found the learning process started by the activity worth any harshness on

DO THE “EYES” HAVE IT? 191 8 that day. I think that follow-up sessions to the activity are crucial as an emotional and psychological debriefing to the intensity of the activity so that people don’t become too overwhelmed. . . . While I am still trying to decide exactly how I feel about the process of the activity, I do think that it is immensely important. I think that ways of further looking at the issues should be explored so that people who participate can make the necessary changes within themselves if they are willing. Because of the importance of fighting all types of discrimination, I think that the activity might need to be changed some in order to encompass this. Overall, though, this is a highly important process of changing attitudes and behaviors that the activity begins. (White female, blue-eyed) Elliott’s exercise closes with recommending activities and readings concern- ing racism and anti-racism to exercise participants. However, it is usually left to the individual participants to grapple with the issues raised by their experiences in the exercise and to choose to further their diversity awareness or to lapse back into old patterns. Organized follow-up sessions coordinated by individuals with expertise in teaching anti-racism are advisable to ensure that diversity awareness is enhanced and not impeded by participation in Elliott’s exercise. The impor- tance of viewing Elliott’s exercise as merely a first step toward assisting Whites in coming to terms with their White Identity and dealing with personal and insti- tutional racism was taken quite seriously by the counseling staff at the college where the exercise was evaluated. As described in the introduction, these individ- uals organized and implemented the follow-up workshops for students who par- ticipated in the exercise. Tatum’s (1 997) book Why Are All the Black Kids Sitting Together in the Cafeteria? and Other Conversations About Race provides a num- ber of helpful antiracism techniques that might be implemented to ensure that participation in Elliott’s activity leads to improved rather than degraded inter- group relations. Future research might further address the impact of negative emotions, as well as other potential mediators, on White exercise participants’ attitudes toward members of other ethnic groups in both the short term and the long term. A Question of Ends Justifying Means Even though Elliott’s exercise is associated with prejudice reduction, and even if appropriate follow-up is provided, do the benefits of the activity justify the costs to the participants? Whereas the vast majority of participants in both the blue-eyed and brown-eyed groups reported being glad that they had participated in the activity, the blue-eyed participants, who received discriminatory treatment, were less likely to report that they would recommend participating in the activity to others. While blue-eyed participants’ reaction could be a result of empathy for

191 9 STEWART ET AL. others who might experience what they went through, this pattern of responses for participants in the discriminated group is also consistent with the classic the- ory of cognitive dissonance (Festinger, 1957). Reporting regret at having partici- pated in a harsh and stressful exercise for which they received little tangible reward would likely yield considerable dissonance for participants in the group that received the worse treatment. However, these participants could indicate reservations about the exercise through expressing reluctance to recommend the activity to others without engendering the same dissonance associated with eval- uating their own participation in the exercise. Additional evidence of the emotional costs of the activity is the choice of 2 White exercise participants to discontinue project participation because they found the exercise too distressing. As previously reported, 1 blue-eyed partici- pant fled the exercise midway through participation because of the stress of the situation. Byrnes and Kiger (1990) noted that the stress of both the participants and the simulation facilitators should be carefully considered in deciding whether or not to implement prejudice simulation exercises such as Elliott’s: Even if the outcome was geared toward laudable ends (i.e., emotional role playing to empathize with oppressed members of a minority group), was the exposure to ridicule and unfair treatment, and giving ridicule justi- fied? What were the risks to a participant’s self esteem? . . . The simula- tion facilitator, too, experienced stress. The facilitator must discriminate against some participants as part of the activity. Acting in a cold, uncaring manner and maintaining that role are contrary to the typical stance any facilitator would take toward students. (pp. 353-354) Elliott herself has commented on the stress she experiences in preparing for and conducting the activity. Several of the present authors experienced consider- able stress in relation to the role of recruiting participants who underwent emo- tional strain and discomfort far greater than anything expected by most in this role. This stress was exacerbated by the authors having no control over the way in which the exercise was conducted (an essential component of an objective pro- gram evaluation), although they had recruited participants to take part in the exercise. In the interest of ethical treatment of participants, a thorough under- standing of facilitators’ prejudice simulation techniques, as well as knowledge of APA ethical guidelines, is recommended for anyone who might consider recreat- ing this emotionally charged diversity training exercise.
